projectOutComesReport:
Metallic glasses are a unique class of metals with structures very different from the more common crystalline materials. Whereas atoms in most metals are arranged in a regular, ordered pattern, metallic glasses have a disordered atomic structure, similar to the liquid state. This difference at the atomic-level often results in dramatically different properties at the large scale, including higher strength, better corrosion resistance, and a surprising ability to be easily and inexpensively molded into complex shapes. Not all metals are able to form glasses, however. Recent studies suggest that the ability to form a glass may be related to the atomic structure of the high temperature liquid. Unfortunately, quantitatively describing the disordered atomic structure of the liquid in order to predict the glass forming ability of a metal alloy is challenging, since there is no long-range pattern to the atomic positions. Previous attempts to identify common polyhedral shapes in the liquid atomic structure are instructive. However, they offer limited insight into the degree of similarity among those shapes and therefore the overall degree of structural order, particularly for alloys consisting of multiple elements of different atomic sizes. This project instead used artificial intelligence-based algorithms to automatically identify structurally 'similar' atomic clusters in computer-simulated metallic liquids and disordered solids. This approach revealed that these structures were made up of a surprisingly small set of characteristic 'building block' atomic clusters. The population distribution of these building blocks in the liquid and their similarity to crystal-like structural features were shown to correlate very strongly with glass formation observed experimentally across several metal alloy compositions, providing a method to identify potential glass forming alloys without experimental trial-and-error. The project also examined how the building blocks in simulated glasses changed with mechanical deformation. Some building blocks were found to be very stable, changing very little with deformation, while the atomic arrangement of other building blocks fluctuated significantly. For the first time, these results suggest a way to clearly define 'defects' in the disordered atomic structure. In crystalline materials, such defects are responsible for many material properties, such as strength. Planned future investigations will attempt to control the defect population in metallic glasses in order to improve their properties.

This work established a method to accelerate the discovery of new, high-performance metallic materials for a variety of applications, as well as contributed to the development of a science and engineering workforce trained in computational and efficient manufacturing methods. Two PhD students and three undergraduate students were trained in the research techniques employed in this work. The work also resulted in a new educational module on the structure and properties of glassy materials.

abstractText:
Non-technical Abstract:
The way in which electrons move through materials determines many of the fundamental properties of any system, such as conductivity or reflectivity. In most materials, however, these properties are qualitatively the same whether we consider one electron in isolation, or many moving in concert. More subtle and interesting effects can arise if the electrons interact with one another, in which case emergent behaviors appear that cannot exist for just one or a few electrons: a simple analogy is that ocean waves are the coherent motion of vast numbers of water molecules. Yet connecting the microscopic behavior of interacting electrons to the overall behavior of a material is often challenging. In this work, the principal investigator uses measurements of infrared light shining through thin materials to probe the behavior of interacting electron systems in several interesting cases. These include ultra-clean graphene devices, comprised of single-atom-thick sheets of carbon atoms in which the electrons interact to generate fascinating many-particle quantum states. These devices are also placed in small cavities to greatly amplify the intensity of the infrared light; under these conditions the electrons and waves of light are thought to merge into novel quantum states that forget their origins as separate entities. Finally, in some materials the electrons interact so strongly that none can independently move; yet they are free to rotate in a correlated fashion to yield fascinating, fluid-like behaviors. This physics is exceedingly difficult to isolate and probe, but recent theoretical work suggests that infrared light can discern whether such a fluid-like state is present. In addition, the principle investigator leads diversity initiatives within the Physics Department that are leading to an increase in Latino/a graduate students. These efforts are being coupled to bridge programs operated in the university at large and also by the American Physical Society, toward making the faces in the physics community more representative of the nation as a whole.
  
Technical Abstract:
Systems of many interacting particles are both fascinating and enigmatic, exhibiting macroscopic correlated behaviors that are often poorly understood. In this project the principle investigator explores correlated electron physics using infrared magnetospectroscopy, which acquires a novel sensitivity to many-particle interactions when applied to materials that have a linear band structure or non-parabolic dispersion. Such linear systems were once incredibly rare but now arise in multitudes of modern quantum materials. The principle investigator utilizes a dedicated infrared magneto-spectroscopy capability to study graphene and strongly correlated materials in fields up to 14 T and temperatures approaching 100 mK, with optics capable of working with microscopic samples of atomically-thin materials. Upgrades will further enhance signal-to-noise, resolution, and spectral range. This enables explorations of three distinct but inter-related projects: first, spectroscopy of electron-electron interaction effects in the integer and fractional quantum Hall regimes in graphene, toward elucidating their role in symmetry breaking and formation of many-particle ground states. In the second project, these graphene devices are placed in mirrored cavities having a resonance in the infrared to enhance the interaction of light with the cyclotron resonance transitions in graphene. This is predicted to achieve the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics, vaulting graphene to the forefront of systems hosting strongly interacting light and matter. Moreover, the uneven spacing of graphene Landau levels implies a proper two-level system is achievable, presaging a novel graphene-based qubit operating in the infrared and native to high magnetic fields. In the third project, strongly correlated insulators including SmB6, YbB12, 1T-TaSe2 and 1T-TaS2 are explored. These materials are thought to host an unusual Fermi surface of neutral spinons, specifically predicted to exhibit novel cyclotron resonance modes.

abstractText:
With this award, the Chemistry of Life Processes Program in the Chemistry Division is funding Dr. John-Stephen Taylor at Washington University-Saint Louis to develop methods for establishing the existence and locations of G-quadruplexes in cells. The double-helical B-DNA structure discovered by Watson and Crick revolutionized the understanding of how genetic information is replicated and expressed as RNA and proteins in cells.  G-quadruplexes are labile four-stranded DNA structures that have more recently been found, along with other non-B-DNA structures, to add new dimensions to the fundamental understanding of how the expression of genetic information is controlled.  The study uses a unique reaction of G-quadruplexes with light that leads to indelible and unique molecular imprints in DNA.  These distinctive imprints provide direct evidence for the existence of G-quadruplexes in cells, allowing their positions and dynamic behavior to be investigated within the human genome. The existence of G-quadruplexes and other non-B DNA structures lead to better understanding of their roles in disease development. Graduate students working on this project receive multidisciplinary training in synthetic organic chemistry, photochemistry, automated DNA synthesis, molecular and cellular biology, and mass spectrometry.  In addition, teaching modules and tutorials for high school students are developed that use physical and computer models to understand G-quadruplex structures and how their photochemistry differs from that of standard B-DNA.   

This project builds on a long-standing program in the principal investigator's laboratory to use chemical and biophysical tools to study the details of complex nucleic acis structures, with a particular focus on G-quadruplex structures.  The scientific approach takes advantage of the observation that UV irradiation of G-quadruplex-forming sequences containing thymine (T) and cytosine (C) bases in adjacent lateral loops results in the formation of stable anti-cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (anti-CPDs), photoproducts that cannot form in canonical B-DNA.  Highly sensitive methods are developed to detect these anti-CPDs photoproducts in cells using post-labeling and isotope dilution mass spectrometric methods. Their positions within the genome are located through ligation-mediated polymerase chain reaction (PCR) methods.  Structure-photoreactivity relationships that serve as unique molecular signatures of G-quadruplexes and other related non-B DNA conformations are determined using enzyme-coupled mass spectrometry assays of site-specific isotopically labeled DNA.  The broader impacts include presenting research opportunities to students from traditionally underrepresented communities and the development of new materials to teach concepts of DNA structure that align with educational standards.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of this project was to develop new methodology for identifying and locating the presence of unusually folded structures of DNA, the genetic material of life, inside living cells.  These unusually folded DNA structures are of great interest because they are hypothesized to play important roles in the controlling the functions of cells.  It has been very difficult to establish the existence and location of these structures in living cells, however, because of their transient nature.   We had hypothesized that we could trap these fleeting structures by using a pulse of ultraviolet (UV) light to irreversibly cross-link remote (non-adjacent) parts of their folded structures together, thereby allowing them to be identified and located in a spatial and temporal manner.  To this end we developed a highly sensitive method for identifying the existence of such cross-linked structures by degrading the DNA with enzymes to a small non-adjacent cross-linked molecules that could be labeled with radioactive material so that they could be detected at very low levels.  Attempts to detect the formation of these non-adjacent cross-linked molecules following irradiation of human cells have so far not succeeded, possibly due to their much lower abundance than expected.  We therefore also developed an alternative method for detecting the same non-adjacent cross-linked molecules using mass spectrometry instead of radioactivity and have validated it for model systems but have not yet in cells.  Lastly, we investigated the use of a sequencing technology based on measuring the current changes when a single DNA molecule passes through a small pore (nanopore sequencing) to determine the location of non-adjacent crosslinked DNA.  We expected that the non-adjacent cross-linked DNA would be prevented from passing through the nanopore whereas adjacent cross-linked DNA arising from normal DNA would not be but would substantially alter the current.  At this point we have been able to detect single adjacent cross-links formed in normal DNA, as well as tandem adjacent cross-links that cannot be assayed by existing methods.  More work will be needed to determine if unusually folded DNA structures can be identified by nanopore technology.

The two analytical techniques that we developed for the identification of non-adjacent crosslinked DNA photoproducts will enable researchers to probe for the involvement of certain types of non-B form DNA structures in model systems and in living cells.  The ability to sequence adjacent cross-linked photoproducts in single DNA molecules using nanopore technology will facilitate studies of the formation and repair of adjacent crosslinked DNA induced by sunlight that can lead to skin cancer.  Another potential application of our methodology is for probing the structure of the RNA which is produced from DNA by determining the formation and location of adjacent and non-adjacent RNA crosslinks by nanopore sequencing. The methods we developed for assaying UV-crosslinked DNA should also be applicable to the study of the folding and interactions in DNA-based materials. 

As part of this grant, we also developed tutorials for high school and university students that are freely available on the web to help better understand the structure of normal and folded DNA through the construction of accurate 2D and 3D models of DNA from card stock and by computer modeling.  The 3D models employed magnets to mimic the H-bonding interactions that hold DNA together thereby allowing students to explore various possible ways in which DNA can assemble and fold.  The tutorials also illustrate how UV light can be used to crosslink the folded DNA structures and thereby provide information about the structure of the DNA from which they arose.  We also created interactive 3D computer modeling-based tutorials of various normal and folded DNA structures with instructions on how to create one's own 3D modeling tutorials.  These approaches to understanding DNA structure were also disseminated to local high school teachers through a hands-on workshop and have been used in courses taught by the PI at the undergraduate and graduate level.

This NSF grant has resulted in three peer reviewed publications, with two additional manuscripts in preparation.  A website was also created that contains all the tutorials and instructional material for the preparation of 2D and 3D models, as well as interactive computer-generated 3D molecular modeling tutorials.  This grant also supported the training of three PhD students (one of which is from an under-represented minority) and one undergraduate.  Two of the PhD students received joint training between the PI and a biological mass spectrometrist.  All three PhD students presented their work multiple times at international and local meetings which enabled them to network with researchers from academics, government, and industry thereby strengthening their interest and commitment to pursuing careers in science.   Two PhD students are continuing their PhD studies, the other is pursing postdoctoral studies in photobiology, and the undergraduate is planning to attend graduate school in chemistry.

abstractText:
Part I: Nontechnical
The geology beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet sets up a key condition to its moving glacial systems: a weak, porous, and possibly water bearing sedimentary layer provides a slippery bed, whereas hard basement rock at the contact may reduce the ice flow. Knowing the geology, however, has been extremely difficult since the continent is remote and the ice cover is thick. Using seismic stations deployed on top of the ice sheet provides an alternative tool to see the continent through the ice, as seismic signal they record contains sensitive information about the base of the ice-sheet and the geology of the crust below. For example, a thick and porous sedimentary layer will cause the seismic waves to travel more slowly. In this project, the investigators will 1) utilize the seismic data collected in the past 18 years at more than 200 sites in Antarctica, 2) perform a suite of modern seismic data analysis tools to produce a variety of seismic signals, and 3) translate them into sets of maps about the physical properties (such as the speed of the seismic wave) and chemical composition (such as silica content) of the underlying crust. These seismic speed maps, with accuracy quantified by uncertainty measurements, provide a first-order assessment to the distribution of the sub-ice sedimentary layer. Additional information such as other crustal properties and inferred chemical composition beneath these sites will further shed light on the geological evolution of the continent buried by the thick ice sheet. Notably, determining the silica content of the crust will help produce better estimates of  the thermal profiles of the sub-ice crust.  

Part II: Technical Description
The underlying crust of Antarctica Ice Sheet holds strong importance from perspectives of both cryosphere and lithosphere: at local and regional scale, the shallow physical properties at the base of the Antarctic Ice Sheet sets an important boundary condition for the dynamics of the fast moving ice sheet; at a greater scale, the architecture (thickness and Poissons ratio) of the crust that varies across the continent retains the signature of the past geological evolution and its chemical composition contributes significantly to the geothermal structure. However, these properties have not been systematically studied due to both the remoteness of the continent and its thick ice-coverage. In this proposed study, the investigators will analyze 18 years of seismic records from more than 200 permanent and portable seismic stations, to constrain the sub-ice seismic structure, crustal architecture, and draw implications on the chemical composition of the bulk crust using multiple seismic techniques. Their analysis will include: 1) systematic measurement of the broad-band Rayleigh wave horizontal-vertical ratios (H/V) from both ambient noise and earthquakes; 2) analysis of high frequency receiver function waveforms and 2-layer h-k stacking to provide information on Poissons ratio and the depth of sub-ice discontinuities; 3) measurement of Love wave dispersion and inversion for radial anisotropy; 4) measurement of Rayleigh wave azimuthal anisotropy from both ambient noise and earthquakes; 5) Joint interpretation of Rayleigh wave dispersion, H/V ratios, and receiver function waveforms for detailed sub-ice isotropic structure; 6) a Monte Carlo transversely isotropic (TTI) modeling of all seismic anisotropic measurements. These analyses will be combined and synthesized to produce a set of seismic deliverables including the determination of a map of thickness of the sub-ice sediments with hierarchical-resolution, more accurate crustal thickness and Poissons ratio determination, and quantification of crustal composition. The proposed work will meet two major scientific objectives. First, it will provide detailed information about the bottom contact of the Antarctic ice-sheet and sediment thickness at localities of seismic stations, improving the boundary conditions for the ice-sheet modeling and determining the locations of major sedimentary basins within Antarctica. Second, constraints on the thickness and composition of the Antarctic crust will improve the understanding of the geology history of the continent. Notably, the crustal architecture and composition will further facilitate future geological investigation to various tectonic processes that have shaped Antarctica, such as rifting, lithospheric removal, orogeny, and mountain building.

projectOutComesReport:
The crust and upper mantle structure of Antarctica has been poorly understood, due to the remote location and thick ice cover. While most previous studies have focused on the isotropic structure, this project investigated the seismic anisotropy structure beneath central and west Antarctica.   Seismic anisotropy is the directional dependence of seismic wave velocity resulting from the directional variation in elastic constants.  Since the directional variation in elasticity is usually caused by deformation, we can use seismic anisotropy to  better understand the deformation history of the crust and mantle.  We used all broadband seismic records collected in Antarctica over the past 20 years to investigate the shear wave anisotropy structure. We founs positive radial anisotropy (horizontally polarized shear waves travel faster than vertically polarized waves) in the shallow crust and a few places in the mid-to-lower crust, likely due to the orientation of the mica-bearing rocks. Much of the lower crust shows negative anisotropy, likely due to the lattice preferred orientation of plagioclase. The uppermost mantle generally has positive anisotropy, with the largest magnitudes beneath the Transantarctic and Whitmore Mountains, where it likely results from tectonic activity.    

We also investigated shear wave azimuthal anisotropy, the variation of shear wave velocity with azimuth.   We found that a two-layer anisotropic structure fits the study region, with different azimuthal variations in the upper crust and the mantle. In West Antarctica, the fast direction of crustal azimuthal anisotropy aligns with the extension direction of the West Antarctic Rift System. The agreement between our results for the uppermost mantle and teleseismic shear wave splitting studies suggests a thin lithosphere or similar lithosphere-asthenosphere deformation.

In addition, the improved shallow resolution of this project allowed us to determine a new continental-scale sediment thickness map, which reveals a thick sediment layer beneath the Southeastern Ross Embayment. Basins on the interior of the continent show sediment and sedimentary rock thicknesses of less than 1.5 km.   The lack of thick interior sedimentary basins is likely due to sediment-starved conditions through much of the basin history, due to variable arid conditions on the interior of the Antarctic continent.

abstractText:
Non-Technical Description: 
The basis of all modern electronics relies on multilayered materials composed of semiconductors. Here, the investigators are developing instrumentation to determine the specialized chemical structures and the 3-dimensional forms in interface regions where different semiconductor layers are in contact with one another. These methods combine laser excitation with nuclear magnetic resonance detection to provide atomic-level information critical to improving the performance of these modern electronic devices. This project includes collaboration with the National High Magnetic Field Lab and will impact semiconductor device fabrication industries. The research innovations are integrated with multidisciplinary courses offered at Washington University for educating and training students. The collaboration also provides new research networks for team members, enhancing the professional development of students and postdoctoral researchers. Informal science education activities for high school teachers are offered through the Institute for School Partnership.

Technical Description: 
This research interrogates the structure of semiconductor interfaces by using enhanced signals that are created through optical pumping of conduction electrons. Optical pumping in the optically pumped nuclear magnetic resonance (OPNMR) localizes the detected signal to interfacial regions and greatly enhances the sensitivity, transforming NMR from a bulk to a surface technique. In collaboration with the National High Magnetic Field Lab, laser access and NMR sensitivity are improved by utilizing a new coil design based on high-temperature superconductors that permits unimpeded laser access and higher performance than conventional solenoids. Such spectroscopy can enable engineering of devices by revealing the underlying makeup of the interface, and examining strain induced by defects, lattice mismatch, and dopants. Model structures of GaAs coated with deposited metal oxide thin films, such as alumina and hafnium dioxide are probed. The OPNMR is developed to adapt these methods for studying other metal-oxide semiconductor devices to examine the role of defects in Fermi-level pinning at this interface. This information is critical to improving performance of metal-oxide semiconductor devices. The high polarization achieved is utilized to measure the magneto-optical penetration depth and ultimately the nuclear polarization. To date, these values have only been estimates but are crucial for understanding the observed spins and the effectiveness of the optical pumping, explicitly using nuclear spin temperature.

projectOutComesReport:
This research project has aspirations to drive new developments in the combination of magnetic resonance techniques (specifically "nuclear magnetic resonance" or NMR) with optical techniques.  By using photo-excited electrons in semiconducting materials, the constituent atoms in the vicinity of the excited electrons can be manipulated -- their spin orientation, their relaxation properties (e.g., their return to an equilibrium state), and importantly their population, in order to enhance these signals for analyses via their spectra (their signature appearance, using magnetic resonance). 

The application area for research of this type is to study semiconductors, materials that make up modern electronic devices (including laser pointers, photo-detectors, and LEDs). In particular, there is a strong desire to better understand the structures present at the interface between layered semiconductor materals which have a vanishly-small number of atoms to observe.

The specialized technique under development shines laser light onto the surface of these semiconducting materials which -- under very specific conditions -- creates electrons that are oriented according to opto-electronic states.  Those states also interact with nearby atoms that possess nuclear spin, an intrinsic property of the isotope, making it amenable to magnetic resonance.

This project was aimed at building new hardware to better study these phenomena and permit exploratory studies.  The research also was deeply enaged in understanding the appearance of complicated nuclear spin signals arising from CdTe semiconductors (probing the 113Cd and 125Te species) and layered materials with GaAs, coated by AlGaAs or AlxOy, probing any combination of 27Al, 69Ga, 71Ga, 75As, all of which are "quadrupolar" isotopes, meaning they have nuclear spin values that are greater than 1/2 -- imparting special interactions that lead to additional insights of structure and surrounding electronic environments.

This research was first launched still during the COVID-19 pandemic.  With limited access to the lab for the initial phase, the group at that time switched efforts to computational and simulation tasks (for species with 27Al present) and of CdTe that are described below.

Model CdTe was explored to better understand the manner in which the different atoms in the lattice of this crystalline material interact under the effects of laser irradiation, followed by NMR detection.  There are two different isotopes that are active in NMR experiments, and these are 113Cd and 125Te. The signals exhibit behavior that suggest one isotope is sensitive to how the other spin interacts with the optically-generated electrons and the surrounding lattice.  In probing the time-dependent behavior of these signals -- as various experimental variables are manipulated-- we are developing ways to better understand how the lattice acts to dissipate these magnetic resonance signals.  Because this is computationally-intense work, many simulations and models have been tested and developed during this project, and we are still on the verge of finalizing the last manuscript from these efforts.  Our models of the phenomena are complex, and we continue to try to finesse them to provide the most thorough understanding of the interacting spins.

In collaboration with the National High Magnetic Field Lab, a new piece of magnetic resonance equipment, called an "NMR probe", was envisioned.  What NHMFL brought was a unique structure to both deliver and collect these magnetic resonance signals -- termed a "coil".  The coil is often shaped like a spring (or "solenoid"), that the sample can sit within for analysis, but the spring shape would cause scattering of the incoming laser light.  This new design is unprecedented in the area of optically-pumped NMR, and this new probe was built and tested on GaAs, as a proof-of-concept.   This new magnetic resonance equipment is poised for studies of layered structure of semiconductors with optical pumping of the sample space (at high magnetic fields) for the first time.

We have also had success creating a catalogue of some of these quadrupolar species, using computational methods to predictively calculate the experimentally measured data, based on crystalline structures.  That database now resides in a portion of The Materials Project, for 27Al NMR.

The project overall has led to notable outcomes for the graduate student and postdoctoral researcher involved.  The graduate student went on to a medical physics lab, where optical pumping is being employed for gases, for MRI lung imaging of children and infants.  The postdoc researcher also was able to launch his independent career in a tenure-track position in a physics department at a "Research 1" institution.  Finally, this project and the lab it supports is part of the Washington University Center for Quantum Leaps, founded since the inception of this project, to support researchers from multiple disciplines to collaborate on areas related to quantum information and sensing.  Hayes is the lead PI of an NSF NRT training grant on this topic, in large part due to the confluence of this research and opportunities to enhance learning in quantum-related areas.

abstractText:
Non-technical Abstract:
The way in which electrons move through materials determines many of the fundamental properties of any system, such as conductivity or reflectivity. In most materials, however, these properties are qualitatively the same whether we consider one electron in isolation, or many moving in concert. More subtle and interesting effects can arise if the electrons interact with one another, in which case emergent behaviors appear that cannot exist for just one or a few electrons: a simple analogy is that ocean waves are the coherent motion of vast numbers of water molecules. Yet connecting the microscopic behavior of interacting electrons to the overall behavior of a material is often challenging. In this work, the principal investigator uses measurements of infrared light shining through thin materials to probe the behavior of interacting electron systems in several interesting cases. These include ultra-clean graphene devices, comprised of single-atom-thick sheets of carbon atoms in which the electrons interact to generate fascinating many-particle quantum states. These devices are also placed in small cavities to greatly amplify the intensity of the infrared light; under these conditions the electrons and waves of light are thought to merge into novel quantum states that forget their origins as separate entities. Finally, in some materials the electrons interact so strongly that none can independently move; yet they are free to rotate in a correlated fashion to yield fascinating, fluid-like behaviors. This physics is exceedingly difficult to isolate and probe, but recent theoretical work suggests that infrared light can discern whether such a fluid-like state is present. In addition, the principle investigator leads diversity initiatives within the Physics Department that are leading to an increase in Latino/a graduate students. These efforts are being coupled to bridge programs operated in the university at large and also by the American Physical Society, toward making the faces in the physics community more representative of the nation as a whole.
  
Technical Abstract:
Systems of many interacting particles are both fascinating and enigmatic, exhibiting macroscopic correlated behaviors that are often poorly understood. In this project the principle investigator explores correlated electron physics using infrared magnetospectroscopy, which acquires a novel sensitivity to many-particle interactions when applied to materials that have a linear band structure or non-parabolic dispersion. Such linear systems were once incredibly rare but now arise in multitudes of modern quantum materials. The principle investigator utilizes a dedicated infrared magneto-spectroscopy capability to study graphene and strongly correlated materials in fields up to 14 T and temperatures approaching 100 mK, with optics capable of working with microscopic samples of atomically-thin materials. Upgrades will further enhance signal-to-noise, resolution, and spectral range. This enables explorations of three distinct but inter-related projects: first, spectroscopy of electron-electron interaction effects in the integer and fractional quantum Hall regimes in graphene, toward elucidating their role in symmetry breaking and formation of many-particle ground states. In the second project, these graphene devices are placed in mirrored cavities having a resonance in the infrared to enhance the interaction of light with the cyclotron resonance transitions in graphene. This is predicted to achieve the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics, vaulting graphene to the forefront of systems hosting strongly interacting light and matter. Moreover, the uneven spacing of graphene Landau levels implies a proper two-level system is achievable, presaging a novel graphene-based qubit operating in the infrared and native to high magnetic fields. In the third project, strongly correlated insulators including SmB6, YbB12, 1T-TaSe2 and 1T-TaS2 are explored. These materials are thought to host an unusual Fermi surface of neutral spinons, specifically predicted to exhibit novel cyclotron resonance modes.

abstractText:
Stretching for over 80 miles along the Illinois bank of the Mississippi River, the area of Mississippi River Floodplain known as the American Bottom is home to over 130,000 people who depend on infrastructure that controls and curtails flooding. Although the Mississippi River is the most the significant threat to floodplain communities in the American Bottom, a system of floodplain channels has triggered some of the most widespread and damaging incidents of flooding. In some cases, substantial infilling with sediment and woody material has caused these channels to literally pour into some of the most economically vulnerable communities in the US. In this EAGER proposal, the investigators will apply a new model in the practice of geomorphology, in which scientists and community members collaborate in inquiry and data collection. They will focus their initial efforts in the community of Centreville, Illinois, where the impacts of flooding have been the most damaging. They will work directly with the community to better constrain the causes and impacts of severe flooding, and to broaden their engagement with communities of the Greater St. Louis region, they are partnering with Harris-Stowe State University to offer four summer internships to rising seniors of the university. Their goal is to build meaningful and empowering undergraduate research experiences for underrepresented minorities by designing those experiences around civic engagement and environmental science.

The investigators aim to demonstrate how community-centered research that is applied to managed and inhabited landscapes can, at the same time, lead to novel and impactful insights into landscape evolution. In their case, the focus is on floodplain channels of the American Bottom. Floodplain channels have been a focus of research in geomorphology for some time, but these previous efforts have largely focused on floodplain channels whose very forms are produced and controlled by lowland rivers. Floodplain channels whose forms and function are largely independent of lowland rivers, but instead are a product of upland drainages, are much less understood. The investigators will provide the first geomorphological assessment of the floodplain channels of the American Bottom, including both natural and modified reaches. By integrating field surveys, sediment coring, and numerical experiments the investigators will: 1) calculate sediment supply rates from bluff drainages into floodplain channels; 2) determine how and why sediment transport capacity varies along floodplain channels; and 3) identify flood risks associated with channel infilling for Centreville.

projectOutComesReport:
Centreville, IL has suffered pervasive flooding for decades. However, to date, no action has been taken towards mitigating these hazards and their associated economic and social impacts on the community. Regular flooding in Centreville has persisted, nearly daily in some neighborhoods, for almost two decades without mitigation or intervention. Spring and summer floods have required public evacuations (last covered by popular press in 2015), and persistent flooding in some neighborhoods has waterlogged homes to such an extent that county officials have condemned some residences. The frequent and pervasive flooding in the Centreville community, paired with the lack of any mitigation efforts due to the lack of adequate "return on investments", represents a clear example of environmental injustice in Centreville.

A key need articulated by residents during our first meeting was for the comprehensive documentation of the conditions that drive flooding in the neighborhood, as well as documentation of flood frequency and flood extent. While residents have relayed their personal experiences of flooding to state agencies, due to limited resources and lack of infrastructure, no concrete or systematic documentation of flood hazards was available.  Guided by community needs and resident experiences, in 2020 we installed ten time-lapse cameras throughout the community to continuously monitor flood extent. Installed cameras captured one photo and a 5 second video every 30 minutes at each location. We also installed two pressure transducers to monitor water levels every five minutes in a small channel that runs through the community and drains the nearby bluffs. Qualitative analysis of these ground-based time lapse images clearly demonstrates that Centreville residents experience frequent, severe flooding, even under moderate precipitation conditions. Correlation of individual ponding events with daily precipitation records suggests a precipitation threshold of between 0.5-1 inches/day to initiate severe surface ponding across the community, though moderate ponding was often observed below this threshold. 

We also developed and calibrated a hydrologic model using the Hydrologic Engineering Center-River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) developed by US Army Corps of Engineers to estimate flood extent under a range of precipitation scenarios. We demonstrate that inundation is widespread even under moderate precipitation rates across the community, consistent with findings from field-monitoring efforts.   We also show that the precipitation threshold identified from images was consistent with rapid increases in inundation as predicted by the calibrated flood model at the camera locations. We also find that our calibrated flood model reflects areas where water will pond due to topography, but that existing FEMA flood models of the 1% flood do not capture the flooding that we model or observed from the field-monitoring efforts.

While these results were consistent with residents lived experiences, they help to demonstrate these experiences and the severity of flooding experienced by the community through direct observations and modeling. Community-engaged cooperation with data collection efforts guided the project scope and field-based efforts significantly, allow our team to focus areas of the community where flooding was most pervasive and damaging to resident?s properties and day-to-day life.  Results of this work support mitigation efforts sought by residents and community partners.  As part of these efforts, we cooperated with the community partners working to support these efforts to seek environmental remediation and relief for residents from nuisance flooding. We advocate for a community-engaged model for future studies of urban monitoring and modeling. Additionally, as part of this project, we provided two, eight week research internships to students from Harris Stowe State University, a St. Louis HBCU.

abstractText:
The COVID-19 pandemic has confronted researchers with unprecedented challenges. One of these challenges is the need to determine whether ongoing or new research projects are essential to conduct in-person during the crisis, and if so, which research personnel should conduct this research. Such decisions have been made all the more difficult by the challenges that plague them, including extreme time pressures, insufficient or vague guidance, competing personal and professional trade-offs, and uncertain ramifications for those affected by these decisions. A thorough understanding of the ethical and practical dimensions of these decisions is needed to help researchers and institutional officials better prepare for managing the scientific workforce during future crises. This project aims to understand how principal investigators have made these decisions during the current pandemic and identify the factors in their environments that shaped their decision-making, and how these decisions impact research personnel in their lab (e.g., graduate students, postdocs, technicians, staff scientists). Data from this project can help improve understanding about how principal investigators might approach challenging decision-making during similar future situations and how research personnel perceive and are affected by these decisions. Fostering enhanced awareness of and deepened appreciation for the unique challenges such emergencies pose to essential researchers will be valuable for researchers and the broader community that benefits from their work.

This project addresses two primary research questions: 1) what ethical considerations and practical challenges shape principal investigators’ decision-making about whether and how to conduct in-person research projects during the COVID-19 pandemic?, and  2) how do research personnel ethically appraise their PI’s decisions and decision processes in light of their relationship and the context of the pandemic? Data collection will proceed using a mixed-methods approach to synthesize quantitative survey-based information from principal investigators and research personnel and interviews with select researchers, graduate students, and research staff. Initial surveys will be completed by hundreds of NSF- and NIH-funded scientists and research assistants, and follow-up interviews will be conducted with select participants. Data will then be synthesized, analyzed, and interpreted. Findings will be disseminated widely to benefit researchers in future emergencies. Answering these questions contributes to the research on ethical decision-making, ethical research cultures, research leadership, and pandemic policy-making.

projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic presented unprecedented circumstances for principal investigators (PIs) and their research teams. Research had to be abruptly suspended with only research activities deemed essential continuing in-person. Guidance was limited and changing, which put PIs in the position of making difficult decisions that affected members of their research teams and their research programs. PIs? decisions had implications for the fair treatment of research personnel and their safety, the ethical treatment of research subjects, and responsible stewardship of valuable research resources. These decisions also had personal and career consequences for PIs and affected the continuation of the scientific endeavor.

We conducted a national survey of PIs funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Research personnel completed a corresponding survey. The PI survey examined how PIs prioritized different considerations when making decisions about conducting and staffing research that continued in-person, on-site. Overall, PIs prioritized research personnel wellbeing and considered the perspectives of personnel when making their decisions. Personnel views of their PIs? decision processes and outcomes were generally congruent with PI views. Personnel perceived PIs as being fair and having communicated well about the decisions made. However, there was some variability among personnel in their perceptions.

We also examined PIs? views about factors that helped or harmed their ability to make these choices effectively. PIs tended to perceive more factors that helped them make decisions relative to factors that harmed their ability to make decisions. Factors that especially made PI decision making more challenging included when personnel lacked childcare or were at high risk for COVID-19 complications. PIs also found it more difficult to make decisions when institutional guidance was too vague or conflicting. Factors that PIs perceived as supporting decision making included having research personnel who would speak up with concerns and positive research group dynamics. Across survey responses, early-career PIs? concerns and perceptions varied relative to PIs who were more senior. Early-career PIs rated concerns about their careers and productivity as more salient in their decision making compared to their mid- and late-career counterparts. Early-career researchers also reported perceiving more factors that harmed their decision making compared to more experienced researchers.

To gather detailed information about the experiences of PIs and personnel, we conducted in-depth interviews with a subset of PIs and research personnel who completed the survey. The findings suggest important actions PIs can take to create resilient and psychologically safe research environments when normal research operations are upended. Such actions include explicitly encouraging feedback from personnel and integrating this feedback into decision making, being transparent about why certain decisions are being made, and trusting and empowering research personnel to help solve problems.

Broadly, institutional leaders and PIs can utilize what was learned from this study to prepare for future circumstances by developing contingency plans and policies that better support research teams in crisis situations. Ideally, institutional leaders would consider both professional and personal needs of PIs and research teams when developing guidance and providing resources in crises. A balanced approach may also be required in which guidance provides general principles but also grants autonomy and flexibility in determining the specific implementation of guidance within research teams.

abstractText:
This award is made under NSF's EAGER funding mechanism, which supports Early-Concept Grants for Exploratory Research. Some data-intensive digital agriculture technologies have been in use in farms and other food production operations since the 1990s. The range of digital agricultural technologies is now expanding rapidly and some of these technologies are being introduced more widely. Historically most agricultural technologies have brought impacts beyond the obvious realms of yield and farmer profits, including impacts on technical knowledge, on dependencies, and relations among farmers. Given the diversity in emerging digital technologies and in the settings into which they are being introduced, such indirect impacts will be highly diverse and difficult to predict. To date, most research on digital agriculture has focused on a narrow set of issues, with scant attention to indirect impacts and little analysis from a comparative perspective. This EAGER project will conduct exploratory pilot research in diverse settings to collect data to allow investigators to develop a comparative, multi-sited study of this range of impacts. The project is appropriate for EAGER funding because it aims to collect data to test and evaluate questions as a step towards developing a proposal for the larger comparative project.

Interviews will be conducted by a team of researchers with local knowledge of agriculture across multiple sites and scales. While the specific digital technologies and farmer characteristics will, by design, vary greatly across sites, researchers will investigate four sets of related questions in each setting. The first concerns identifying the recipients of information about farm operations and farmer behavior. Potential recipients include private companies, government offices, extension agents, CGIAR researchers, and academic analysts. Each of these has distinct expertise and sets of interests. The second concerns the social dynamics of adoption and non-adoption. Farmer decisions on adoption may be driven by various factors other than simple bottom-line profit expectations. The third concerns effects on farmer behavior. The last concerns effects on social relations among farmers.

abstractText:
The project will develop new statistical methods to analyze stochastic phenomena that inherently evolves in time. The methods will be based on high-frequency monitoring of the phenomena under study, which is of widening use in many fields such as finance, meteorology, biology, neuroscience, turbulence, statistical physics, seismology, and telecommunication. Thus, the research will foster more interaction between applied scientists and statisticians. The research and educational elements of the project will also serve as a training tool for both undergraduate and graduate students by forming synergistic research groups involving all levels. 

Nonparametric methods are powerful statistical tools to reduce the model misspecification error, and high-frequency-based statistical analysis is a natural route to take when estimating the fine statistical features of continuous-time stochastic processes. Though the literature combining these two approaches has grown significantly during the last two decades, comparatively little work has been done to analyze and correct the sensitivity of methods to tuning parameters. The project will address these needs by (i) developing a unified approach for optimal kernel estimation of the spot volatility of an Ito process in the presence of leverage and microstructure noise; (ii) devising of optimal jump detection and integrated variance estimation methods, under the presence of stochastic volatility and infinite jump activity, via thresholding or shrinkage of the process' increments or wavelet coefficients; (iii) establishing theoretical guarantees for the data-driven plugging implementation methods resulting from the optimal schemes.

projectOutComesReport:
The three general primary directions of the grant are the following:

(R1) Developing a unified approach for optimal kernel estimation of the spot volatility of an Ito process in the presence of leverage and microstructure noise;

(R2) Devising optimal jump detection and integrated variance estimation methods, under the presence of stochastic volatility and infinite jump activity, via thresholding or shrinkage of the process' increments or wavelet coefficients;

(R3) Establishing theoretical guarantees for the data-driven plugging implementation methods resulting from the proposed optimal schemes.

The following are some proposed educational activities of the project:

(E1) Research experiences for undergraduates and master's students;

(E2) Organization of special sessions in international and national conferences.

 

Summary of Activities:

(1) During the last year, one of the PI's Ph.D. students (Chang Liu) successfully defended his Ph.D. disseration in December 2023. The PI is currently working with two Ph.D. students: Jincheng Pang and Tianwei Zhou.

(2) I directed the undergraduate research of two students: Anna Wang and Thomas Li. Anna will pursue a graduate master program in MIT starting Fall and Thomas will continue during Summer 2024 in his research project. 

(3) We submitted three papers:

(3a) Market Making with Stochastic Liquidity Demand: Simultaneous Order Arrival and Price Change Forecasts (jointly with Chuyi Yu and Agostino Capponi), submitted to SIAM journal of Financial Mathematics (SIFIN);

(3b) Efficient Integrated Volatility Estimation in the Presence of Infinite Variation Jumps via Debiased Truncated Realized Variations (jointly with Yuchen Han and Cooper Boniece), submitted to Stochastic Processes and their Applications (SPA);

(3c) Data-driven fixed-point tuning for truncated realized variations (jointly with Yuchen Han and Cooper Boniece), submitted to Bernoulli.

We received feedback from the three papers, requesting minor/major revisions. The SIFIN paper' revision was submitted and we are finishing the revision of the SPA paper. I will then start revisiing the Bernoulli paper.

(4) The PI organized a mininsymposium in the 2023 SIAM Conference on Financial Mathematics & Engineering, entitled "Inference and Calibration of Financial Models based on High-Frequency and LOB Data". The mini-symposium is strongly connected to the project.

(5) The PI is teaching a course in "Nonparametric Function Estimation" in Spring 2024, which is closely related to the project. 

 

Significant Results:

(1) Related to the direction (R1), the PI proposed a spot volatility estimator based on kernel smoothing that is robust against microstructure noise, which is present in high- frequency data. The asymptotic was developed. One of the most important results is to show that the optimal kernel is the exponential kernel, which, on one hand, sheds some evidence against the use of uniform kernels and, on the other, motivates the study of kernels of unbounded support.

(2) Related to the direction (R2), the PI developed a new estimator for integrated volatility, which is variance and rate-efficient in the presence of infinite jump activity components. This is just the second estimator of this type and Monte Carlo experiments show the proposed estimator exhibits superior performance over the other method.

 

Contributions to Broad Impact:

(1) The researcher's findings are important to gauge the statistical and quantitative implications of sudden shifts (aka jumps) in continuous-time stochastic processes such as stock prices and other financial measurements. The proposed probabilistic models are aimed at providing a better description of real stock prices by incorporating jumps (such as crashes). An empirical assessment of the possible jumps of the underlying assets is critical as these shifts play a key role in implementing appropriate risk management and investment strategies. Furthermore, the incorporation of high-frequency intraday data is crucial, since the developed methods should take into account both the macro- and micro-empirical behavior of asset price.

(2) The main motivation of the project comes from applications in finance, so, the results are expected to be of interest to the financial and econometric community. The studied method may also be translated to other nonparametric methods in statistics.

(3) The PI is committed to educating and exposing graduate and undergraduate students to statistical and computational problems in real applications such as those encountered in the financial industry. He is currently advising 3 Ph.D. students at WashU.

abstractText:
Algebraic combinatorics is an area of research that seeks to build connections between discrete structures and algebraic objects, with broad applications in computing, statistics, biology, and other subjects of mathematics. A central theme in combinatorics problems is to organize discrete data in a way that reflects key structural properties, thereby making it easier to analyze. This project applies the tools of algebraic combinatorics to study solutions of complicated systems of equations, called algebraic varieties. The PI will develop sophisticated counting techniques to streamline computations and decipher patterns in otherwise complex data. The PI then will use geometric properties of algebraic varieties to uncover new approaches to unsolved problems in algebra and combinatorics. In addition this project also provides research training opportunities for graduate students.

The specific research addressed in this project concerns the combinatorial and geometric structure of Hessenberg varieties and extended Springer fibers. Hessenberg varieties are subvarieties of the flag variety whose cohomology rings encode rich algebraic structure. The PI will use topological data obtained from Hessenberg varieties to outline a new approach to the long-standing Stanley-Stembridge conjecture in combinatorics. The geometry and topology of Hessenberg varieties is completely understood in only a few cases. Using combinatorial invariants and an affine paving, the PI will characterize geometric properties of Hessenberg varieties.  Graham has defined an analogue of the Springer resolution, called the extended Springer resolution. The PI will use the fibers of this map to develop a new geometric framework for the generalized Springer correspondence, transforming the usual approach to this seminal work.

projectOutComesReport:
This research program analyzed data from representation theory using techniques from combinatorics—a branch of mathematics concerned with counting, arranging, and studying discrete structures. The primary goal was to determine how many ways such information can be organized. 

Representation theory studies symmetries and encodes them using algebraic information. That information may be simple, for example, the number of points fixed by a specific symmetry, or more complex, such as computing the number fixed point sets with a fixed dimension. This project specifically investigated symmetries on solutions to systems of polynomial equations, focusing on geometric objects known as Springer fibers and their generalizations: Hessenberg varieties and extended Springer fibers.

A central goal of the project was to develop an algorithm to compute a specific representation, whose symmetries are encoded by a Weyl group. This outcome was achieved using discrete data in the form of lists of integers, called Betti numbers, of Hessenberg varieties.This led to a new connection between Hessenberg varieties, the representation theory of Weyl groups, and a fundamental class of symmetries known as the Springer representation. Work is ongoing to develop a combinatorial model that explains the resulting formulas and explore potential applications.  

The project also produced a new geometric framework for a major result in representation theory known as the generalized Springer correspondence. This framework captures additional symmetries not previously accounted for, thereby offering a more complete picture and providing a geometric realization of otherwise abstract concepts. 

In addition to its research contributions, the project emphasized mentoring undergraduate and graduate students, with the goal of increasing the number of students at Washington University in St. Louis who pursue scientific careers. Several publications and related activities directly supported students’ professional development. Over the duration of the award, the project supported the production of 16 research publications. The principal investigator directly mentored 6 undergraduate and 4 graduate students during this time.

abstractText:
Zhengwei Zhang and Dr. Xinyi Liu, of the Washington University in St. Louis, along with colleagues will conduct research to explore the animal-based subsistence strategies in a high altitude extreme environment. Understanding of the development of high-altitude adaptations in has been enriched by recent anthropological investigations. Such studies have revealed specific challenges regarding strategies for securing a reliable food supply in different seasons. The goal of this research is to increase understanding of how to achieve long-term resilience in the context of concerns regarding food security and more frequent extreme climate events. Archaeology is well placed to provide meaningful insights on resilience because it provides information on people’s behaviors over a long time span. This research will promote understanding of the past, as well as the present by documenting invaluable animal resources and resilient strategies in harsh areas, where biodiversity is threatened. Educational and outreach activities will deepen broad scale academic cooperation, as well as facilitate the development of open academic environments. 

By focusing on animal resources that people used at high altitudes, this research explores the ways that societies were able to be more resilient to periodic stresses and to survive despite the inhospitable and unpredictable environment. The researchers will conduct comprehensive study of prehistoric animal remains from one of the world’s most inhospitable areas. The questions of how farming and hunting settlers managed to live year-round in this high altitude region remain largely unanswered and have been obscured by the scarcity of zooarchaeological studies conducted to date. The researchers will combine systematic zooarchaeological and stable isotopes analyses, and regional ethnographical surveys. This research will reveal animal-based subsistence strategies of pastoral groups and investigate at high resolution how they managed livestock and utilized local natural landscapes. This research has the potential to shed light on human communities’ resilience in extreme environments worldwide.

projectOutComesReport:
Recent archaeological investigations have enriched our understanding of human adaptations to high-elevation environments worldwide. The Tibetan Plateau is one of the most challenging environments for humanity, facing high-altitude and hypoxia conditions. By at least 3500 BP, the establishment of multi-resource pastoralism incorporating livestock management and cereal cultivations had enabled the expansion of settlements on the plateau. How early communities managed their livestock to cope with the challenging environments remains unanswered. By engaging with recent discoveries in the southern Tibetan Plateau at the site of Bangga (3000-2000 cal. BP), this research addresses the missing piece of the story. We employed a combined zooarchaeological and isotopic approach to answering two questions: 1) How might environmental conditions have threatened the survival of early herders at the high elevations? 2) How early Tibetan pastoralists managed their livestock to cope with environmental pressures?

 

Our results offer an original contribution in two principal respects regarding the challenge faced by early herders at c. 4000 m a.s.l. and their solutions. We used dental eruption and wear to reconstruct sheep mortality profiles from Bangga. The mortality profiles revealed that more than 60% of the sheep died within the first year. Simulations based on ethnographic data from Tibet suggested the pattern may be the product of high natural lamb death rates in high-risk environments, challenging the conventional interpretation of culling in the context of milk management. This finding indicates that high juvenile mortality threatened ancient sheepherders. To enable insights into herding practices at such a condition, we conducted sequential isotope analyses of archaeological enamel bioapatite of sheep and goats from Bangga. The isotopic results suggested that some sheep and goats were provisioned with groundwater and fodder composed of agricultural products year around. Other animals may have been taken to graze in saline or marsh environments during the summer. These results provide fresh insight into the prehistoric agropastoralism in high-altitude Tibet, where decreased seasonal mobility corresponding to increased provisioning input differs from the extensive approach previously documented at lower altitudes.

abstractText:
The collection of frequencies at which a geometric structure resonates is called spectrum of that structure.  Encoded in the spectrum is a great deal of information about geometric form, which is difficult to extract.  One might ask: How does the sound of a bell determines its shape, or vice versa?  A new approach to the problem of relating geometry to the spectrum, based on a concept called the hypoelliptic Laplacian, has shown great promise. The purpose of this project is to build a new theoretical foundation for the hypoelliptic Laplacian, and then develop its applications in harmonic analysis and elsewhere.  Expected outcomes will include a clearer and deeper overall understanding of the the hypoelliptic Laplacian, and a broadening of the range of applications to which it may be applied.  There will be significant training and mentoring opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in geometric and harmonic analysis, distributed across the three sites involved in the project. 

In more detail, this project will create a foundational theory for Jean-Michel Bismut's hypoelliptic Laplacian as it arises in symmetric and locally symmetric spaces, and elsewhere. For this purpose the investigators will use techniques previously developed in noncommutative geometry, especially the pseudodifferential operator theory originally developed to tackle the local index problem in noncommutative geometry. Turning to applications, in principle the hypoelliptic Laplacian offers a new approach to Harish-Chandra's Plancherel formula for real reductive groups, and an early priority will be to explore this application further.  The newly established Mackey bijection in the representation theory of reductive groups (discovered in noncommutative geometry) will be investigated simultaneously. Many other potential applications in noncommutative geometry present themselves, and these will be studied carefully during the course of the project.

projectOutComesReport:
This grant supported a focused research group studying the Hypoelliptic Laplacian, Noncommutative Geometry, and their applications to representations and singular spaces.

Significant progress has been made on several projects. This progress not only greatly advanced the study of these subjects but also established exciting new connections between different areas of mathematics, including analysis, geometry, and representation theory.

In the project on the Helton-Howe trace, Connes-Chern character, and quantization, the trace invariant was proven to be constant under deformation, and an explicit formula for the trace of the semicommutator of Toeplitz operators was obtained.

In the project on higher orbital integrals and index pairing, explicit formulas for cyclic cocycles on real reductive groups were discovered. These formulas can be viewed as cyclic cohomology generalizations of classical orbital integrals, which are important invariants in representation theory. The pairing between the cyclic cocycles and K-theory led to a new index-theoretic understanding of the character formula in representation theory.

In the project on Bismut's Hypoelliptic Laplacian and its large-time behavior, explicit computations of the large-time asymptotics of heat kernels on homogeneous spaces were obtained for the first time. This computation offered a new geometric approach to the Novikov-Shubin invariants on homogeneous spaces. Furthermore, the understanding of the large-time asymptotics provided the geometric counterpart of Vogan's minimal K-type theory in representation theory.

In the project on the Riemann-Roch-Grothendieck theorem for orbifold embeddings, orbifold singularities were investigated using antiholomorphic flat superconnections on groupoids. Interesting properties of the Chern character of coherent sheaves on a complex orbifold were established for the first time.

This grant offered training opportunities to many early-career researchers. Five undergraduate students, eight Ph.D. students, one master's student, and four postdocs were mentored by the PI. Seminars and workshops were organized regularly each semester. Two conferences were organized in December 2022 and June 2023. In these research activities, leading researchers from around the world discussed important new developments and proposed problems for future research. These events had a broad impact by providing intellectual stimulation for all participants and giving a large group of junior participants the opportunity to interact with senior researchers.

abstractText:
Some bacteria are capable of using electricity and energy from light to fix carbon dioxide and ultimately for renewable, carbon-neutral to carbon-sequestering production of certain high value compounds.  The overall goal of this project is to better understand this bioproduction process and to engineer bacteria to use this process for bioplastic and biofuel production. This project will create immersive research opportunities for students at the high school, undergraduate and graduate school levels. 

Microbial reduction-oxidation reactions drive matter and energy flow in the biosphere. Most microbes use soluble electron donors and acceptors, but some use solid-phase conductive substances. The underlying microbial process is called extracellular electron transfer (EET). The directionality of electron flow during EET can be either outbound, where solid-phase conductive substances are microbially reduced via reductive-EET; or inbound, where solid-phase conductive substances are oxidized via extracellular electron uptake (EEU). While reductive-EET is long studied, EEU has come to fore recently, and represents a paradigm shift in microbial biogeochemistry. This is because EEU-capable microbes can oxidize abundant solid-phase conductive substances such as minerals for microbial growth. A number of microbes can perform EEU, but only a subset of these organisms can perform phototrophic-EEU. This specialized metabolism harnesses the energy of light and electrons from solid-conductive minerals or their proxies (poised electrodes) to fix carbon dioxide. Accordingly, phototrophic-EEU represents a new metabolism to engineer for sustainable, carbon-neutral to carbon-sequestering bioproduction. To understand the environmental prevalence of phototrophic-EEU, and realize its full bioengineering potential, several fundamental knowledge gaps must be addressed. These include in-depth characterization of the electron input modules and their regulation; and the electron transfer pathways and the cellular electron sinks. Using multi-omic and transdisciplinary approaches, this project aims to fill these knowledge gaps to gain a systems-level understanding of phototrophic-EEU in the freshwater microbe, Rhodopseudomonas palustris and the marine microbe Rhodovulum sulfidophilum. The project will use synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, and material science to improve sustainable production of bioplastics and biofuels using phototrophic-EEU. Together, this project will expand our understanding of phototrophic-EEU, and explore the production of sustainable bioproducts using the phototrophic-EEU capable microbe, Rhodopseudomonas palustris. This project will also engage students from various educational levels in sustainability research.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

The research proposed in this project elucidated the molecular underpinnings of phototrophic-EEU, which empowers sustainable bioproduction. Importantly, this project created creative and immersive scientific education opportunities at the high school, undergraduate, and graduate school levels.

The project utilized synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, and materials science to enhance the sustainable production of bioplastics and biofuels using phototrophic EEU. Together, this project expanded our understanding of phototrophic-EEU and explored the production of sustainable bioproducts using the phototrophic-EEU-capable microbe, Rhodopseudomonas palustris. This project also engaged students from various educational levels in sustainability research. Using scientific writing as a method, several high-school, graduate, and undergraduate students were involved in understanding extracellular electron transfer and its role in sustainable bioproduction. The work accomplished in this project lays a solid foundation for future work on this process, contributing to the development of the US bioeconomy.

abstractText:
Understanding of the structure of the four-dimensional universe in which we live is a key topic of investigation in modern mathematics and physics. Gauge theory is a crucial tool for the study of the mathematical structures that provide the context for standard models of the physical world. The research supported by this project will develop new mathematical tools and theories that will help test such models and advance our understanding of four-dimensional spaces. A key mathematical idea is the interaction between three-dimensional theories known as Floer theories and the study of invariants of four-dimensional spaces. In addition the project provides research training opportunities for graduate students.

This project will develop and extend invariants including abelian gauge theoretic models, cobordism invariants arising from the critical values of Morse like functions such as Daemi's Gamma invariant, equivariant extensions such as equivariant singular instanton knot homology, and new parameterized invariants that combine Konno adjunction-style complexes with homotopy invariants of families. It will also translate structures uncovered in some gauge theory packages to other packages, for example translating L-space notions from Heegaard Floer theory to analogues in the instanton case, or equivariant structures from the Seiberg-Witten Floer theory to the Heegaard Floer theory. Topological applications will include new insights into knot concordance, homology cobordism, diffeomorphism groups of 4-manifolds, and SU(2) representations of 3-manifold groups.
