projectOutComesReport:
Overview: Correct assembly and organization of cellular structures is critical for any organism’s healthy function. This project aimed to identify mechanisms that organize major structures on the cell surface of the single-celled protozoan Tetrahymena thermophila. Ciliated protozoans, including Tetrahymena, possess some of the most elaborate cell structure among single-celled organisms, rivaling even the most complex animal cells. Egg-shaped Tetrahymena cells exhibit both anterior-posterior (top-bottom) and ventral-dorsal (front-back) organization of specific surface organelles. Obvious structural features include their ~18 evenly-spaced, longitudinally arranged rows of cilia, which they use to swim, and the oral aparatus (a feeding organelle -- aka the ‘mouth’) located at the top, front (ventral side) of the cell. The knowledge gained through this research provided new understanding into processes that these cells use to assemble structures of correct size, number, and at the proper position on the cell surface. These organelles carry out multiple functions, thus cells that improperly assembly these structures grow poorly and have sub-optimal health. The outcomes of the project are detailed below.

Intellectual Merit: To elucidate how Tetrahymena cells control the number of structures assembled on its surface, we investigated the function of the Broadened Cortical Domain (BCD)1 gene, which when disabled, results in the assembly of multiple ‘mouths’ (a normal Tetrahymena cell has a single mouth) and supernumerary excretory pores. Our studies found that this protein controls surface organelle assembly by regulating vesicle trafficking to and from the cell membrane (E. Cole et al 2024). The identification of the BCD1 gene as a possible regulator of membrane trafficking led us to hypothesize that the highly conserved (found in protists, plants, and animals) cyclic-AMP (cAMP) dependent Protein Kinase A (PKA) signalling pathway is important for ensuring proper cellular organization over succesive cell divisions. Our studies of the PKA protein family in Tetrahymena revealed four related catalytic subunits and five related regulatory subunits, which indicated multiple similar complexes may control different aspects of cellular organization. Focused analysis on two PKA catalytic subunits, which we discovered localize specifically to the cell’s ventral surface, provided evidence that localized PKA signaling ensures that the mouth is correctly built during cell division. First, localization of these two catalytic subunits was displaced in predicted ways in mutant Tetrahymena cells that have altered surface organization. Second, deletion of the gene encoding one of these PKA subunits results in the cells having an elongated mouth, reducing the cell’s ability to feed. Third, deletion of the genes encoding both these proteins caused dividing cells to assemble additional mouths. Thus, PKA signaling is important for regulating the size and number of surface organelles; however, it likely acts downstream of the proteins that set up the initial cell organization. Our efforts to identify downstream targets of PKA signalling revealed that multiple cellular pathways or structures are subject to its control. These include membrane trafficking pathways – supporting our initial hypothesis, protein folding pathways, as well as ciliary basal bodies and the cell’s membrane skeleton, both major structural components of these cells. It became apparent during this project that many signaling pathways are localized near ciliary basal bodies. The project also served to initiate a collaborative research project to uncover the structure of the Tetrahymena basal body at molecular resolution using cryo-EM. These findings of conserved signaling pathways and structures will be of broad interest to researchers who study cellular organization.

Broader Impacts: The project served as a training vehicle for several early career scientists. One research technician, who is a first-generation college graduate currently in graduate school working towards her PhD, was a major driver of the research. A post-doctoral researcher joined the project to lead the structural analysis of Tetrahymena basal bodies. Fourteen undergraduate researchers were engaged in independent research related to the intellectual merits of the project; ten of which were supported by summer internships (seven female and three male). Two students wrote senior theses on their research. Several of these individuals are authors, or will be future authors, on publications from this work. Furthermore, the project supported the work of 50 students in course-based research projects in the PI’s lab course, Biology 3492. Each student web-published their final research papers on SUPRdb.org, an online report database for the rapid dissemination of research results. Of note, two students from the 2021 course made the discovery that PKA localizes to the ventral surface of Tetrahymena, kickstarting much of the work describe under intellectual merit. This fact demonstrates that students in courses can make important scientific discoveries when given the opportunity. The project also initiated the creation of the “Searchable Ciliate”, a comprehensive research resource consisting of engineered Tetrahymena cell-lines made available to the broader research community. This resource has been handed over to the Tetrahymena Stock Center to curate, thereby making these resources sustainably findable and usable by the broader research community.

abstractText:
Low dimensional topology is an area of mathematics that studies qualities of three- and four-dimensional spaces which are insensitive to continuous deformations such as stretching and bending. These spaces model real world objects and low dimensional topology is highly relevant to other scientific disciplines. For example, knot theory, a branch of low dimensional topology, is an effective tool in studying configurations of protein and DNA. In addition, topology plays an essential role in formulating modern theories in physics. Perhaps more surprisingly, tools from modern physics, more specifically quantum filed theory, have yielded significant progresses in low dimensional topology. This National Science Foundation funded project promotes systematic application of ideas in physics to topology and vice versa.  The PI aims to investigate applications of the Yang-Mills theory of high energy physics in the topological properties of three-and four-dimensional objects. The proposed research also partly focuses on foundational questions in symplectic geometry, a field with close ties with Physics.

Instanton Floer homology, defined using Yang-Mills gauge theory, provides algebraic invariants of three- and four-dimensional manifolds. The PI will apply different versions of instanton Floer homology to the study of problems in low dimensional topology. The focus of the first part of the project is the Atiyah-Floer conjecture. This conjecture states that one can apply methods from symplectic geometry to define three-manifold invariants. Furthermore, the resulting invariant, often called symplectic instanton Floer homology, is isomorphic to instanton Floer homology. The PI and his collaborators will develop tools in symplectic topology which can be used to construct new types of symplectic instanton Floer homology. They will also use a certain partial differential equation, called the mixed equation, to address various versions of the Atiyah-Floer conjecture. Another goal of this project is to prove the existence of non-trivial representations of knot groups into the special unitary group SU(N). An outcome of this project would be to give gauge theoretical proofs of the Smith conjecture and the Covering Conjecture. The final goal of this project is to employ instanton Floer homology in the study of the homology cobordism group. The PI recently constructed a family of new invariants for the homology cobordism group using Yang-Mills gauge theory. The PI will apply these invariants to better understand the structure of the homology cobordism group.

projectOutComesReport:
One of the fundamental ideas in geometry and topology is to study spaces by examining appropriate functions defined on them. Morse theory exemplifies this concept, asserting that the topology of a smooth manifold can be understood using a Morse function defined on the manifold. Morse homology, which is defined in terms of the critical points of a Morse function, provides a method to organize the information derived from the Morse function. By considering the values of Morse functions at these critical points, it becomes possible to introduce additional structure on Morse homology in the form of a filtration. Morse homology inspired the construction of a powerful range of tools known as Floer homology, which extends the ideas of Morse homology to infinite-dimensional contexts.

There are several different types of Floer homology in low-dimensional homology and symplectic topology, providing powerful tools in these two fields. The present project focuses on instanton Floer homology in low-dimensional topology and Lagrangian Floer homology in symplectic topology. Instanton Floer homology yields a 3-manifold invariant and is defined by applying techniques of Morse theory to the Chern-Simons functional, which is defined on the (infinite-dimensional) space of all connections. In particular, the values of the Chern-Simons functional provide a filtration on instanton Floer homology. These filtrations are employed by the PI to define an invariant called 'Gamma' for an important family of 3-manifolds. A key property of Gamma is that it is well-behaved with respect to cobordisms between 3-manifolds. On the other hand, Lagrangian Floer homology serves as an invariant for a pair of Lagrangians in a symplectic manifold. In desirable cases, it admits a filtration analogous to instanton Floer homology.

One of the main scientific outcomes of this project is the establishment of a version of the Atiyah-Floer conjecture, which provides a connection between instanton Floer homology and Lagrangian Floer homology. Specifically, given a Heegaard splitting—a decomposition of a 3-manifold—one obtains a pair of Lagrangians in a symplectic manifold. The Floer homology of these Lagrangians, when well-defined, is referred to as symplectic instanton Floer homology. The Atiyah-Floer conjecture states that instanton Floer homology and its symplectic counterpart are isomorphic. In fact, there exist various approaches to formulate (symplectic) instanton Floer homology, and one of these formulations is known as (symplectic) framed Floer homology. Through this project, it has been demonstrated that this particular version of instanton Floer homology together with its filtration is indeed isomorphic to its symplectic counterpart. This result, along with its method of proof, holds promise for various other applications. For instance, Fukaya and the PI use similar techniques to explore Legendrian contact homology of Legendrians in the 1-jet space of a smooth manifold.

Other outcomes of the project include various applications of the invariant Gamma and related tools in low-dimensional topology. For example, the invariant Gamma is utilized to prove that there exist homology three-spheres that bound definite four-manifolds. However, any such bounding four-manifold must be constructed using a large number of handles. This result specifically demonstrates the existence of an integer homology sphere that bounds a homology ball, but the minimum number of handles in any such homology ball is larger than a given integer N. In another project, employing similar tools, it is shown that certain 3-manifolds cannot be embedded in any closed symplectic 4-manifold, thus disproving a conjecture by Etnyre-Min-Mukherjee. Additionally, in a series of collaborative projects with Chris Scaduto, a collection of knot invariants, including the counterpart of Gamma for knots, is defined. Several topological applications of these invariants are presented, such as demonstrating that there exist knots for which the difference between the (positive) clasp number and the slice genus of the knot can be arbitrarily large.


Beyond the scientific outcomes, the project has had broader impacts through dissemination of results and the training of students. The PI presented progress in various talks, made relevant papers accessible on arXiv and submitted them for publication. Graduate students and researchers actively engaged in the project. For instance, the PI organized several reading groups on topics related to the project. The PI also mentored a graduate student who is working on his PhD thesis and already finished a paper based on a problem related to the project.  Additionally, the PI co-organized a summer research program for undergraduate students, providing research experiences in mathematics and focusing on important skills including collaboration, presentations, and report writing.

This project aims to transform microscopy from the current low-speed benchtop system into the first-of-a-kind high-speed miniature/portable device that will enable wearable, handheld applications. The microscope will include many of the currently available separate optical modalities into a single multi-parameter system. The proposed system will retain these modalities with no reduction in performance yet with improved portability, reduction in size, and increased data collection efficiency for functional imaging capabilities. This breakthrough is expected to find broad applications in areas spanning from neuroscience to clinical treatment of cancer, personalized screening of cardiovascular drugs, and management of wound healing. 


The technology developed in this program will significantly expand the scope of multi-parametric PAM beyond basic research in anesthetized of restrained animals. The multidisciplinary nature of the proposed research involving optical and mechanical design, numerical simulation, microfabrication, data processing, instrument development and testing will offer well-balanced training opportunities for all participants.

projectOutComesReport:
This CAREER program advanced photoacoustic microscopy (PAM), an emerging imaging technology that combines light and ultrasound to study blood vessels, oxygen delivery, and energy metabolism in living tissue. The research integrated optical and mechanical design, laser engineering, microfabrication, and image analysis to create new tools for both basic science and clinical applications.

This program achieved several technical milestones. We developed an ultrafast dual-wavelength fiber laser and new image-processing methods that allow PAM to operate at a record speed, enabling real-time imaging in living tissue. We created a wearable PAM device capable of capturing brain activity in freely moving animals. We built a handheld PAM device for microvascular imaging in humans.

The broader impacts of this program extend beyond technology development. These new tools have already been applied to important biological and medical problems. For example, the handheld PAM device has been successfully applied in humans, providing new ways to diagnose small-vessel disease, while the wearable PAM device enables long-term studies of brain blood flow and metabolism in animal models of neurological disorders. Future applications may also include cardiovascular drug testing and wound healing research.

This program also provided training opportunities for students at multiple levels. High-school and undergraduate students gained hands-on research experience, with multiple deciding to pursue careers in biomedical science, while graduate students benefited from coursework and seminars. Together, these research and educational outcomes have strengthened biomedical imaging efforts at Washington University and contributed new tools to the broader scientific community.

abstractText:
Municipal wastewater treatment processes consume significant amounts of energy.   However, the organic materials fed into the waste treatment process offer the potential for energy-positive waste water treatment if this waste organic material can be converted into energy.  A microbial fuel cell is a device that contains special strains of bacteria which consume organic matter in waste water as a fuel to generate electricity and help clean up the water.  Although microbial fuel cells have shown promise for sustainable and energy- positive waste water treatment, their performance is low.  An unconventional way to improve their performance is to integrate the microbial fuel cell device into a cultivation chamber which grows algae from sunlight.   The project will investigate the synergistic aspects the combined algal-microbial fuel cell for its potential to boost electricity production, reduce operating costs by eliminating the external aeration requirement, and remove inorganic as well as organic materials from waste water.  The educational activities associated with this project make use of microbial fuel cell demonstrations to stimulate interest in environmental engineering and waste water treatment topics with undergraduate students, K12 students and teachers, and the public.

The overall goal of the research is to study the potentially synergistic interactions of a microbial fuel cell integrated into an algal bioreactor as a new platform for energy-positive waste water treatment. In this combined system, the algae generate oxygen which is needed by the microbial fuel cell electrode to drive aerobic micro-bioelectrochemical processes, whereas this same process generates carbon dioxide needed by the algae.  This in situ source of oxygen has the potential to intensify electricity generation and eliminate the aeration requirement.  The algae can also remove inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus to help further treat the waste water.  The research has four objectives.  The first objective is to construct a nutrient budget model based on fundamental understanding of the transformation of inorganic and organic nutrient forms within the algal-microbial fuel cell.  The second objective is to examine how different algal species affect the stability of bacteria within the microbial fuel cell electrode and the algal biomass productivity.  Towards this end, metagenome analysis will be used to identify metabolic functions related to different taxa which are critical to process performance.  The third objective is to quantify treatment of organic materials within the algal-microbial fuel cell using mixotrophic algae. The fourth objective is to conduct system development and optimization with different configurations, including scalable systems.  Through these objectives, this research seeks to gain a fundamental understanding of critical algae-bacteria interactions during nutrient uptake and electricity generation, and will also reveal the pathways of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorous transformation via physical, chemical, and metabolic processes.

projectOutComesReport:
Municipal wastewater treatment plays a critical role in environmental protection, but the operation of such treatment plants consumes extensive energy - 3-5% of US electricity is consumed by water and wastewater treatment; recovering bioenergy from wastewater can reduce energy consumption and the carbon footprint of wastewater treatment. This research aims to addresses key challenges to recovery of bioenergy from wastewater and aims to functionally characterize the components to optimize an innovative photo-bioelectrochemical (IPB) system, which will synergistically integrate microbial fuel cells (MFCs) with algal bioreactors, achieving improved contaminants removal and maximizing energy production in the form of bioelectricity and algal biomass. The specific objectives of this project include: (1) Measure transformation of inorganic and organic nutrient forms and identify the metabolic functions which mediate these to construct a nutrient budget and model, and evaluate algal biomass yield under different conditions; (2) Examine how different algal species affect the MFC stability of bacteria and function, and algal biomass yield ; (3) Study if mixotrophic algae can improve net organics removal and overall IPB efficiency; and (4) Conduct system development and optimization with different configurations.

This project was collaboratively conducted by environmental engineers at Washington University in St. Louis (previously at Virginia Tech) and biologists at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee. The members of this inter-disciplinary team have complementary expertise in wastewater engineering, algae, and microbial biology. The research of this project has generated ten peer-reviewed papers in high impact journals such as Water Research, Science of the Total Environment, and Current Opinions in Chemical Biology. The results have advanced our understanding of the interaction between bacteria and algae in IPB systems and explored the optimization and scaling up of IPB systems towards potentially practical applications. During the project, the research scope was expanded to involve separation of algal biomass by different membranes technologies and additional collaborators from Virginia Tech, University of Maryland, and Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University.   

The project has graduated one PhD student and one MS student (who continued to a PhD study at another university). It also partially supported another three PhD students including one African American student. Those graduate students have been trained for performing scientific experiments, analyzing data, preparing manuscripts, and presenting research findings. The project also involved several (female) undergraduate students and high school teachers (funded by NSF REU/RET programs) who conducted summer research guided by the PI and graduate students. The collaborators have met in person and communicated virtually to discuss the project progress. The UW-Milwaukee PI delivered a departmental seminar at Virginia Tech about the research findings of this project. Research results were incorporated into graduate courses such as CEE5164 Environmental Biotechnology and EECE537 Environmental Resource Recovery for broader dissemination.
